subtype: Approach: dividing subjects between two teammates [Action]
passage: Anand and Tanvir had two weeks before the quiz and one long syllabus. On the school terrace Anand took a notebook and drew a line down the middle. "You're better at history and sports, right?" "Yes," said Tanvir. "Then I'll take science and maths. You lead on the other two." They wrote it on the page in big letters. Every evening they swapped one new fact and one puzzle. In the mock round, when a science question came, Tanvir nudged Anand at once, and when a cricket question came Anand nodded to Tanvir. No one spoke over the other, and the clock hardly mattered.

qa.q: How does Anand seem to feel about splitting the subjects?
qa.a: Anand seems confident and organised, drawing a line down the notebook so each person leads where strongest and they avoid clashing over answers.

qa.q: What alternative approach could the pair use if a question comes from an area neither leads, and why?
qa.a: They could agree that the person who feels surer answers or that they whisper and decide together. A simple signal keeps the rhythm during buzzer rounds.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see the split?
qa.a: Tanvir was asked about strengths and got history and sports, so Tanvir probably feels trusted and relieved that the workload is shared.

grounding: A pair decides one will handle science and maths and the other history and sports, saving time and avoiding clashes over answers.

"Salma, we keep answering over each other."
"Because you always buzz."
"Because you always look at me!"
"Okay, okay. Let's split it. Which subjects are you good at?"
"Science. And maths, sort of."
"I'm better at history and sports."
"So science and maths, I answer. History and sports, you answer."
"And general knowledge?"
"Whoever knows first. But we look at each other and nod."
"And if I'm sure about a history one?"
"Then you whisper it to me, and I say it."
Lavanya held out her little finger. "Deal?"
"Deal."
In the next practice they didn't clash once.

qa.q: How did Salma feel at the start of the talk?
qa.a: Salma felt irritated, blaming Lavanya for always buzzing and clashing.

qa.q: What would you change first if the split did not work in a real quiz?
qa.a: They could agree a quick hand signal for who answers, because under pressure a nod is easy to miss.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Salma?
qa.a: Salma gets the strong subjects and a clear role, so Salma feels respected and happy to make the deal.

grounding: It shows a quiz pair dividing subjects between them so they save time and avoid clashing over answers.

subtype: Approach: dividing subjects between two teammates [Action]
passage: When Zeenat and I first practised for the inter-school quiz, it was a mess. We both knew some answers and both started talking at once, and the quiz master took our points away for two answers. So on the bus home, I took out my notebook and wrote two columns. Zeenat: history, sports, films. Vidya: science, maths, animals. General knowledge: whoever is sure, but the other one nods first. We read our columns every evening and only studied our own subjects. On the day we didn't clash once. In the science round Zeenat just sat back and smiled. It was strange, trusting someone else with half the answers, but it worked.

qa.q: Which subjects did Vidya write down as Vidya's own?
qa.a: Vidya wrote science, maths and animals.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel about trusting Zeenat with half the answers?
qa.a: Vidya found it strange and a little uneasy at first, but relieved when it worked.

qa.q: What else could Vidya and Zeenat do to cover each other's weak areas?
qa.a: They could each study one easy part of the other's subjects, so there is a backup if one of them blanks.

qa.q: How does the split look to Zeenat?
qa.a: Zeenat can relax during Vidya's rounds, sitting back and smiling, which suggests Zeenat trusts the plan.

grounding: It shows two teammates dividing subjects so each leads an area, saving time and avoiding clashes over answers.
